title: Roaming sense amp sweeps sixteen bitlines inside their charge-hold window
idea: Reverse the one-amp-per-bitline layout: after charge sharing, a bitline holds its ~100 mV signal for ~1-2 us, so one offset-cancelled sense amp steps through a 16:1 mux, regenerating and restoring each bitline in turn, requested column first. The data waits for the amp instead of each amp waiting for data.
why: Periphery (fact 7): bitline SA area falls ~8-16x, returning ~10-15% of the die to cells; first-column latency unchanged, full-row restore ~16 x 3 ns hidden behind the burst.

title: CCD bitline marches charge packets to one edge charge amplifier
idea: Move the charge to the sensor instead of the sensor to the charge: the bitline becomes a buried CCD channel with 3-phase clock gates, cells dump their charge into it, and packets are shifted (image-sensor style) to one low-noise floating-diffusion charge amplifier at the array edge, then shifted back for restore.
why: Facts 7 and 1: one amplifier per ~512 cells instead of per bitline; CCD charge amps resolve tens of electrons, so Cs could drop from ~5 fF to <1 fF with no 60:1 pillars. Shift speed is the main risk.

title: Write-first read infers old bit from charge the driver supplies
idea: Flip read and write order: a per-column-group write driver forces the opened cell to '1' while a charge integrator measures how much charge it delivered (~0 for a stored 1, ~Cs*VDD for a stored 0); the result is latched and 0s are written back. Latch-type sense amp and separate restore phase merge into one driver/integrator.
why: Facts 7 and 8: removes the cross-coupled SA and equalizer (~30% of SA strip area); the integrator sees full Cs*VDD rather than a ~100 mV charge-shared swing, so 2-3 fF cells suffice.

title: Self-referenced double sampling cancels sense-amp offset and bitline mismatch
idea: Reverse where the reference comes from: sample the bitline after charge sharing onto capacitor A, write a known '1' through the same cell and sample again onto B, then compare A against B in the same comparator so its offset and the bitline mismatch cancel; restore the true value afterwards (MRAM self-reference transplanted to DRAM).
why: Fact 7: SA transistors can be minimum size because the ~10-20 mV offset cancels; SA area -50-60% and ~30% smaller signals tolerated (smaller Cs), at ~5 ns extra read latency.

title: Column-first activation: CAS before RAS opens one row segment
idea: Reverse the RAS-then-CAS order: the column address arrives first and enables only the sub-wordline drivers and local SAs of the 1/16 row segment containing it, so ~512 bits are activated, sensed and restored instead of 8 Kb.
why: Fact 8 (128x overfetch): activation energy per useful bit ~5.9 pJ -> ~0.6 pJ; unopened segments also escape row-hammer stress. Costs ~3% area for segment-enable gating.

title: Negative-capacitance bitline element cancels parasitic bitline capacitance
idea: Reverse the sign of the parasitic: a ferroelectric HZO negative-capacitance element at the bitline foot subtracts from the effective bitline capacitance the cell sees, raising the transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+Cbl) from ~0.1 to ~0.3-0.4.
why: Facts 1 and 7: a 3x larger sense signal lets Cs drop to ~2 fF (AR ~25:1) or bitlines grow 3x longer (SA count /3). Hysteresis-free transient NC is the risk.

title: Chopped dither comparator reads signals below its own offset
idea: Reverse noise's role: a tiny comparator fires 16 times in ~2 ns with a known dither added and its inputs swapped every other decision; an up/down counter shared per 8 bitlines cancels the offset (it flips sign with the chop) while the dither linearizes, recovering the sign of a signal far smaller than the offset.
why: Facts 7 and 1: comparators ~0.3x today's SA area still resolve ~10 mV, enabling ~2 fF cells; energy of 16 micro-decisions is below one full latch swing on a long bitline.

title: Victim-margin metering: measure hammered neighbors instead of counting aggressors
idea: Reverse row-hammer defense: on a random 1-in-64 activation, the SA strip re-senses the two neighbor rows with a reference shifted by ~30 mV; only if a bit fails the shifted reference (margin eroded) is that victim refreshed, so no per-row activation counters exist.
why: Fact 9: removes per-bank counter SRAM/CAM tables (several % of periphery) and refreshes only truly degraded victims, robust even at ~1k-activation thresholds.

title: Idle sense amps run backward as distributed charge pumps
idea: Reverse the latch's job: during standby and refresh gaps, two extra switches per SA reconfigure the cross-coupled latches plus bitline capacitance into a distributed switched-capacitor doubler that tops up VPP/VBB right beside the wordline drivers.
why: Facts 7 and 10: central charge pumps and their decap (~5-8% of die) shrink, and local generation removes IR drop on the 3 V wordline rail.

title: Back-gate the array so wordlines swing at logic voltage
idea: Reverse which terminal does the work: a buried, separately biased plate under the access transistors sits negative during retention (raising Vt, cutting leakage) and pulses positive only in the selected subarray, so wordlines need ~1.2 V swing instead of ~3 V and drivers become thin-oxide core devices.
why: Facts 10, 7 and 3: wordline driver area -50-60%, wordline CV^2 energy ~-80%, VPP pump removed; deeper retention bias trims the leakage tail.

title: 3D DRAM staircase rebuilt as the wordline-driver farm
idea: Rearrange the dead staircase of stacked 3D DRAM: each step landing hosts vertical-channel transistors grown in the same deposition steps as the tiers, acting as tier-select and local wordline drivers, so the contact region becomes active periphery.
why: Facts 2 and 7: the staircase is ~10-15% of 3D array area; reusing it as drivers shrinks the CMOS needed under the array and the contact count routed to it.

title: Token-passing row sequencer replaces the random-access row decoder
idea: Reverse random access into order: for AI-weight and KV-cache streaming parts, rows open as a token shifts one wordline per step through a shift-register chain with a small jump table, deleting the NAND-tree row decoder and its pitch-limited predecode buses.
why: Fact 7: row decoders ~8-10% of die -> ~1-2%; activations pipeline back-to-back and decode power drops ~90%; random access survives at bank granularity.

title: Spend periphery to buy back the capacitor: 16-cell bitlines
idea: Reverse the classic trade of long bitlines to save sense amps: use 16-cell bitlines (Cbl ~0.4 fF) with SAs placed under the array, so a planar or shallow ~1 fF capacitor gives the same transfer ratio a 5 fF pillar gives today.
why: Fact 1: eliminates the 60-75:1 pillar etch and exotic high-k; capacitor module steps -30-40%. Requires SA-under-array at ~4x today's SA density.

title: Fuse-less DRAM: host controller holds the repair map
idea: Reverse who repairs: the die ships without fuse/antifuse banks or address-compare redundancy logic; failing rows and columns are recorded in a signed on-module SPD map at test, and the memory controller or OS remaps them to spare rows at boot.
why: Fact 7: removes fuse banks, redundancy comparators and post-package-repair circuits (~3-5% die); spare rows become ordinary capacity when unused.

title: Stepwise adiabatic restore returns bitline charge to tank rails
idea: Reverse the charge flow on discharge: bitlines are charged and discharged in four steps through intermediate tank-capacitor rails, so charge falling from VDD returns to the tanks instead of ground and restore draws only the top step from the supply; dummy array edges serve as tanks.
why: Fact 10 (CV^2 floor): bitline and restore energy -50-70% with 4 steps, without lowering VARY.

title: Periphery wafer on top in leading-edge logic, array beneath
idea: Rearrange the stack: an array-only wafer is hybrid-bonded face-to-face at ~0.5 um pitch to a periphery wafer made in a 3 nm-class GAA logic process, so SAs and sub-wordline drivers are ~5x denser than DRAM-process periphery.
why: Facts 7 and 4: periphery footprint fits under the array, die area -35-45%, array wafer drops ~20 masks. Known in NAND as CBA; new with logic-node periphery.

title: Decoding moves to the controller; DRAM receives one-hot row lines
idea: Reverse where address decoding happens: a logic base die performs row predecode and sends one-hot group-select lines through dense hybrid-bond pads to each array tile; the DRAM die keeps only the final AND gates at the wordline drivers.
why: Fact 7: row/column decoder and address-latch area (~6-8%) leaves the DRAM die; logic-node decode is faster and lower power.

title: Resonant bitline reads the stored bit as a frequency shift
idea: Reverse voltage sensing into frequency sensing: each bitline forms part of a resonator; turning on the access transistor loads it with the cell's state-dependent MOS-varactor capacitance, and one wideband counter reads the detuning of 64 bitlines tuned to separate tones.
why: Facts 7 and 8: one reader replaces 64 SAs, and a probe amplitude far below the stored voltage makes the read non-destructive, eliminating restore energy.

title: Voltage-to-time sensing with one TDC shared by 32 bitlines
idea: Convert the signal domain: each bitline drives a current-starved inverter whose delay encodes the ~100 mV signal; edges from 32 bitlines are serialized into one shared time-to-digital converter that also outputs a margin value.
why: Fact 7: per-bitline hardware shrinks to ~2 transistors; the margin output feeds retention-aware refresh (fact 3).

title: Sense-amp latches become CPU-addressable cache, array the backing store
idea: Reverse the roles of periphery and array: SA latches become low-leakage retention latches that hold a row for milliseconds, tags live in the controller, and the open rows of all banks (tens of MB) serve as a directly addressed last-level cache; the array is touched only on misses.
why: Facts 5 and 8: 60-80% hit rates cut activations ~3-5x and access energy ~50%, and shrink the host's SRAM LLC.

title: Array stores its own sense-amp offset trims, refreshed as charge
idea: Reverse who serves whom: at power-up BIST measures each SA's offset and writes 4-bit trims to a reserved row per subarray; at every refresh that row is read into tiny charge-storage trim capacitors at each SA, which bias the latch to cancel offset.
why: Fact 7: minimum-size SAs with offset trimmed to <3 mV; SA area ~-40% and required signal ~-30%, allowing smaller Cs.

title: Bitline segments become a SAR DAC for two bits per cell
idea: Rearrange the bitline into a capacitive DAC: it is cut into binary-weighted segments switched in successive-approximation steps around the SA, resolving four charge levels per cell in two comparisons, with restore through the same segments.
why: Density x2 with no new cell and no separate DAC area; per fact 1 the margin is tight, so it pairs with offset cancellation or larger Cs.

title: Sparsity-biased precharge: assume zero, sense only departures
idea: Reverse the neutral mid-rail reference: for AI tensors where most bits are 0, bitlines precharge to the 0 level and a single-ended detector fires only when a cell pulls the bitline up; rows dominated by 1s are stored inverted with a flag bit.
why: Facts 10 and 8: bitline swing and restore energy scale with the fraction of 1s, -50-70% for sparse data; single-ended detector ~half SA area.

title: Pitch-split: off-pitch periphery moves to U.S. 200mm chiplets
idea: Rearrange periphery by pitch-criticality: only bitline SAs and sub-wordline drivers stay on the array die from a U.S. memory fab; pumps, regulators, DLL, I/O, ESD, command logic, test and fuses move to a chiplet from U.S. 200mm/130-65 nm lines, attached face-to-face at a U.S. OSAT such as Amkor Arizona.
why: Fact 7 and capital: ~20-25% of die area returns to cells; the off-pitch half runs on fully depreciated U.S. fabs with zero EUV.

title: SiGe bipolar global sense amps on a U.S. BiCMOS chiplet
idea: Reverse the amplifier family: local bitlines pass their signal through one array-side gain transistor onto global bitlines at 8x relaxed pitch, which cross hybrid bonds to SiGe HBT sense amps on a chiplet from a U.S. BiCMOS line (e.g., Vermont); HBT Vbe matching (~1 mV) beats MOS (~10-15 mV), and the milligrams of germanium per wafer can come from U.S. zinc refining.
why: Facts 7 and 1: ~10x lower offset allows 4x longer bitlines (SA count /4) or ~40% smaller Cs, all built domestically.

title: Cross-fab sequential build: U.S. logic fab first, memory fab last
idea: Reverse the wafer-flow order: a U.S. logic fab builds periphery FEOL and a Mo-based interconnect, then ships wafers to a U.S. memory fab that grows the array above at <=450 C with laser-recrystallized Si access devices and MIM capacitors, giving monolithic CMOS-under-array across two U.S. companies without bonding.
why: Facts 7 and 4: die area ~-35% with logic-grade periphery, no HKMG module in the memory fab and no bond-yield loss.

title: Interference lithography for arrays, multibeam e-beam for periphery
idea: Reverse which region gets premium patterning: perfectly periodic array lines are printed by simple laser interference lithography (buildable in the U.S.) and pitch-split with U.S.-made deposition/etch, while the sparse, irregular periphery layers are written maskless by U.S.-built multi-column e-beam.
why: Fact 4: replaces 5-7 EUV layers and mask sets with an all-U.S. toolchain, removing the single-supplier EUV dependency.

title: Bottom-up Mo fill from Colorado moly replaces periphery tungsten
idea: Reverse fill direction and metal: periphery contacts, wordline straps and local interconnect are filled bottom-up by area-selective molybdenum CVD nucleating on the contact floor (no liner, no seams), with precursor refined from U.S.-mined molybdenum.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) removed; Mo's lower narrow-line resistance (~30-50%) speeds wordline drivers and drops liner steps.

title: Image sensor run backward: pinned-diode memory with floating-diffusion readout
idea: Reverse the pixel: in a U.S. CMOS image-sensor fab, a 4T pixel's fully depleted pinned photodiode stores electrically injected charge instead of photo-charge; reading is complete transfer to a floating diffusion and a source follower onto the column with correlated double sampling, and reverse transfer restores the bit.
why: Fact 3: pinned-diode dark current gives seconds-scale retention (~100x less refresh); fact 1: no tall capacitor and a gain-buffered readout. ~10-14F2 cells suit energy-bound tiers.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory: cool the DRAM, shrink the sense amps
idea: Reverse the thermal assumption: memory sleds run at 77 K in liquid nitrogen produced on site by U.S. air-separation plants (no helium); junction and GIDL leakage collapse, mobility roughly doubles and Vt mismatch tightens, allowing half-size SAs and VARY ~0.6 V.
why: Facts 3, 10 and 7: refresh power ~0, CV^2 energy ~-60%, SA area ~-40%; avoids the helium chokepoint entirely.

title: Sense-amp latches drive silicon-photonic rings, skipping column decode
idea: Reverse the data path: instead of SA -> column mux -> global I/O -> PHY, groups of SA latches directly drive micro-ring modulators on a silicon-photonics layer from a U.S. photonics fab (e.g., New York), bonded over the array, with 64 wavelengths per waveguide carrying the row out.
why: Fact 5: data movement ~1 pJ/bit vs 3-20 pJ/bit; the global I/O tree (~5-8% of periphery) disappears.

title: High-voltage drivers on glass: TFT periphery on U.S. panels
idea: Reverse the substrate for high-voltage periphery: global wordline drivers, level shifters and pumps, which need 3-5 V rather than density, are built as TFTs on a U.S.-made glass interposer panel and connected to the array die through fine-pitch redistribution.
why: Fact 7 and capital: thick-oxide periphery (~8-10% of die) leaves the silicon; panel processing costs ~1/10 of silicon per area.

title: Silicon switched-capacitor PMIC replaces on-die charge pumps
idea: Reverse where high rails are made: VPP, VBB and VARY come from a U.S.-fabbed silicon switched-capacitor converter on the module, fed through bumps; silicon is chosen over GaN because gallium is ~98% Chinese.
why: Facts 7 and 10: ~5-8% die area recovered and pump efficiency ~30% -> ~85%, cutting VPP energy ~2.5x.

title: Test brains live in the probe card, not every die
idea: Reverse where DFT lives: test-mode logic, BIST engines, compression and burn-in controllers are stripped from the DRAM die and implemented once on an ASIC in a U.S.-made probe card, reaching the array through a thin raw-access port.
why: Fact 7: ~2-4% die area recovered on every die; test logic is amortized over millions of dies and upgradable without a respin.

title: CHIPS-funded open DRAM periphery IP for every U.S. fab
idea: Reverse the IP model: a government-funded consortium publishes silicon-proven SA, decoder, pump and PHY hard macros with layouts for U.S. mature and memory fabs as open IP, so periphery becomes public infrastructure and companies compete on arrays.
why: Capital and U.S. manufacturability: periphery is ~40-50% of new-DRAM design cost; lowers entry for U.S. memory startups.

title: Merchant periphery wafers: U.S. array startups build only arrays
idea: Reverse vertical integration: one U.S. fab sells known-good periphery wafers with a standard hybrid-bond map, while startups and national labs fabricate only array wafers (~20 fewer masks) in small U.S. fabs and bond them domestically.
why: Capital intensity: an array-only line could cost ~1/3 of a full DRAM fab, multiplying U.S. supply sources.

title: Sense amps built from the array's own vertical transistors
idea: Reverse the borrowing: instead of the array borrowing logic transistors, SAs and sub-wordline drivers are built from the same vertical-channel 4F2 pillars as the access transistors, in the same steps and pitch-matched under the bitlines, so one U.S. memory fab runs the full flow with no logic module or partner.
why: Facts 4 and 7: ~8-12 fewer masks, SA strip area ~-30%, whole die in one U.S. fab.

title: NEMS relay power gates zero out idle subarray periphery leakage
idea: Reverse electronics to mechanics for slow switches: bank and subarray periphery power gates, toggled only on wake/sleep, are nanoelectromechanical relays from a U.S. MEMS foundry layer bonded above, giving true zero off-current.
why: Idle power: idle-bank periphery leakage (~20-30% of standby) -> ~0; ~1e9 lifetime switch cycles suffice for power gating.

title: One sense-amp layer serves every tier via vertical bitlines
idea: Rearrange the scaling direction: in monolithic 3D DRAM grown with U.S.-built deposition and etch tools (no EUV), bitlines run vertically through N tiers to a single SA layer below, chosen by tier-select transistors, so periphery stays constant while bits grow N-fold.
why: Facts 7 and 4: periphery share falls roughly as 1/N with tiers; density comes from deposition, not U.S.-unavailable lithography.

title: Self-timed sense amps signal completion, absorbing mature-node variation
idea: Reverse the timing source: each SA group raises a dual-rail done flag when its latch has regenerated and the bank proceeds when all flags are up, so periphery built at U.S. 28-40 nm fabs runs at typical rather than worst-case speed.
why: Fact 7 and U.S. manufacturability: ~30% timing guardband removed, making mature U.S. nodes viable for DRAM periphery.

title: Sense amps on the wafer backside via U.S. backside flow
idea: Rearrange the faces: using a U.S.-developed backside-processing flow (the kind built for backside power), the array occupies the front, the wafer is thinned, and SAs and wordline drivers are built on the back, joined to bitline groups by nano-TSVs.
why: Fact 7: the front side holds only cells (die ~-30-40%), and the backside also carries power, freeing front metal.

title: Block-copolymer self-assembly draws sense-amp fins at bitline pitch
idea: Reverse lithography's role: coarse guides from U.S. interference or e-beam litho steer U.S.-made block copolymers to self-assemble the 20-30 nm fins of SA transistors at exactly the bitline pitch, so SAs pitch-match open bitlines without folding.
why: Facts 4 and 7: replaces EUV on SA-pitch layers and keeps 6F2 open-bitline SAs pitch-matched, SA area ~-20%.

title: Wide-and-slow periphery lets U.S. 65 nm logic drive DRAM
idea: Reverse speed for width: the array die exposes 8x more data bonds at 1/8 the clock (e.g., 4096 bits at 800 MT/s) to a face-bonded base die from a U.S. 65-90 nm fab; serialization happens only on the host link.
why: Facts 5 and 7: high-speed periphery that forces advanced nodes disappears from the DRAM; I/O energy ~0.5 pJ/bit.

title: Resist-free periphery via area-selective deposition, no imported photoresist
idea: Reverse subtractive patterning: periphery contacts and vias are formed by depositing only where wanted, using area-selective deposition with self-assembled inhibitor monolayers from U.S. chemical suppliers and one coarse e-beam template, eliminating several resist-litho-etch loops.
why: Supply chokepoint: advanced photoresist is ~90% Japanese; also removes ~3-5 litho steps from the periphery flow.

title: Wafer-scale memory slab: one periphery per quadrant, no packaging
idea: Reverse die and wafer: a whole U.S.-fabbed 300 mm array wafer becomes one memory appliance with stitched global buses, redundant reticle tiles and one shared periphery/I/O tile per quadrant, mounted directly on a U.S.-made cold plate with no dicing or offshore packaging.
why: Fact 7 and U.S. manufacturability: per-die pads, I/O and ESD (~10%) amortized; Asian OSAT dependency removed; ~TB per wafer.

title: Measure first, wire last: e-beam personalizes each wafer's periphery
idea: Reverse design-then-build: after array test, a U.S.-built multibeam e-beam writes the final periphery metal per wafer, setting SA reference trims, bitline segmentation and timing taps to that wafer's measured leakage and Cs distribution.
why: Facts 3 and 7: per-wafer tuned margins cut refresh ~30-50% and add ~5-10% yield, deleting on-die trim and fuse circuits.
